html:
No Time to Type

Have you ever tried to write code with a leash in one hand? I don’t recommend it.

Half the Answer: /remote-control

The session runs on my machine. I steer it mostly by dictating into my phone.

The Other Half: Rigor Without Watching

BDD for real, the same way every time: Gherkin, red, code, green, commit.

Asking Nicely? Probably Not.

Instructions are advisory, so hooks enforce the order. I read the record afterward.

Notice that an agent calling an API needs the same thing: controls that still hold when nobody is watching. hooks.json

/remote-control

Please give me an update

Red run logged. Writing the fix.

How’s it going?

Green. Commit gate: TDD order checked.

🐕 pulling. back in 20

Illustrative, not a transcript. The two questions are the real ones, every evening. So is the dog.
say: Have you ever tried to write code with a leash in one hand? I don't recommend it. Between family and a new dog, the time I used to spend at a keyboard is gone. Half of the answer was Claude Code's /remote-control. The session runs on my machine, and I steer it mostly by speech-to-text dictation into my phone, from wherever I am. Most evenings I send two messages: 'Please give me an update' and 'How's it going?' Fair enough, but that's only half. An agent I can't watch needs the three R's before anyone else's does: it has to follow BDD for real, and it has to do that the same way every time: Gherkin first, a red run, the code, a green run, and only then a commit. Can you get that by asking nicely? Probably not. Instructions to a model are advisory. So hooks enforce the order: a write out of turn is refused, every run is logged, and the commit gate checks the order before anything lands. I don't watch the agent; I read the record afterward. Notice that this is exactly what an agent calling an API needs, too: controls that still hold when nobody is watching. So who's really in charge here?
